newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO peacekeepers raid Bosnia war crimes suspects.
newsitem.headline: NATO peacekeepers raid Bosnia war crimes suspects.

text.p: NATO-led peacekeepers shot dead a Bosnian Serb police chief suspected of war crimes on Thursday and whisked another suspect to The Hague to face trial.
Diplomats said the moves reflected an international decision to get tougher on obstacles to peace in Bosnia.
President Bill Clinton commended the action, telling reporters during an official visit to Warsaw: "It was the appropriate thing to do."

U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said the swoops put other suspected war criminals on notice they would not remain free indefinitely -- a pointed warning to the biggest fish still at large, Bosnian Serb wartime chief Radovan Karadzic and army commander General Ratko Mladic.
The European Commission had earlier ratcheted up pressure on Karadzic, saying it was cutting off aid to the Bosnian Serbs until he was arrested.

In a statement, External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek said the arrest of Karadzic, the former Bosnian Serb president who still wields heavy behind-the-scenes power, was required by the Dayton peace agreement.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana warned hardline Bosnian Serbs not to retaliate for the death of Simo Drljaca, the former police chief of Prijedor who was killed when he fired on soldiers trying to arrest him on war crimes charges.
A British trooper was slightly wounded in the operation to apprehend Drljaca, who led brutal ethnic cleansing operations against Moslems and Croats in northern Bosnia in 1992.
Prijedor hospital director Milan Kovacevic was arrested in a parallel operation and was hurried out of Bosnia and delivered to the U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague.
Although the two men's names were not on the official list of war crimes suspects published by the tribunal, a Western official in Sarajevo said they had been mentioned in sealed indictments.
The former Serb mayor of the Croatian town of Vukovar was seized last month under similar circumstances and is now in jail in The Hague.
NATO denied peacekeepers had broken their own ground rules and hunted the men down although the raids, codenamed "Operation Tango", showed every sign of careful planning.
Spokesman Colonel Steven Rausch said they were carried out on direct orders from NATO commander General George Joulwan and Secretary General Solana.
The unprecedented NATO action sent shock waves through the nationalist Serb leadership in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo.
Bosnian Serb television, under the control of Karadzic, struck a tone of panic. "What we were afraid of happened, the threats from the international community materialised," the television said.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, locked in a power struggle with Karadzic, said Drljaca was shot at his home where he lived openly with NATO's knowledge.
Prijedor police said Kovacevic was arrested at the hospital by four NATO soldiers who he said bluffed their way into the building before drawing guns.
Police said Drljaca's 17-year-old son and brother-in-law and who were with him have not been seen since.
NATO insisted the action did not signal a shift in its policy to seize suspects only when encountered in the course of their peacekeeping patrols.

But diplomats said Thursday's move reflected growing frustration in Western capitals at the continuing presence of accused war criminals in Bosnia who retain major influence in politics and block reconciliation of Serbs, Moslems and Croats.

They noted at recent meetings -- of NATO ministers in Sintra, Portugal and government chiefs at this week's summit in Madrid -- that NATO governments had sent stronger messages than before about the need to bring in dozens of indictees at large.
These messages were directed, they said, at peace-keeping commanders on the ground in Bosnia who have considerable leeway in how aggressively they seek out "encounters" with war-crimes suspects.
German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe told reporters in Bonn that Thursday's operation had conformed to the mandate laid down for the stabilisation force.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook Cook also defended the right of the troops authority to carry out such operations against alleged war criminals and said he was proud of the performance of the British forces who staged the raids.
